_note: Elevations are approximate published reference figures. Pass affiliations verified against Epic/Ikon 2025-26 rosters (see README for sources) for major North American and European anchors; entries marked pass_confidence:'verify' change season to season and should be checked at the official pass site before a user buys anything. resort_url is each resort's official site (bulk-verified via HTTP check); snow_report_url is a third-party live snow report, also verified. snotel_triplet is null where no NRCS station exists within a representative distance (most of the eastern US, most of BC/coastal Canada, everywhere outside North America) — those resorts rely on the Open-Meteo forecast panel only. microclimate_note is a resort-specific climate/geography detail (elevation, aspect, storm-track position) distinct from the region-level ENSO/NAO narrative — grounded in real research for the flagship resorts, sound orographic reasoning for the rest. Each region's enso_signals has three variants (el_nino/la_nina/neutral) — app.js picks the one matching data/oni.json's current phase. Two regions (Northeast US/Eastern Canada, European Alps) are NAO-primary — see nao_signals and primary_driver.

el_nino.narrative: El Niño's subtropical jet targets California's coast with unusual persistence. High-elevation resorts consistently outperform — they sit above the rain-snow phase-change zone, a critical distinction when the airmass is warmer than normal.
el_nino.caveat: Snow level is the key variable. A storm delivering 2 ft of water may produce rain at 7,000 ft and powder above 9,000 ft. Always check the forecast freezing level.

la_nina.narrative: La Niña shifts the storm track north, leaving California's subtropical jet largely dry. The Sierra still catches occasional atmospheric rivers when a system dips far enough south, but the reliable pattern favors the Pacific Northwest instead.
la_nina.caveat: La Niña seasons are more boom-or-bust here than El Niño seasons — a handful of big atmospheric-river events can still produce an above-average year. Don't write off California entirely; just expect more variance.

neutral.narrative: With no strong ENSO signal pulling the jet stream one way or the other, California's season is driven more by individual storm luck than by a seasonal pattern. Historical range is wide in neutral years.
neutral.caveat: Watch atmospheric river forecasts week to week rather than leaning on a seasonal thesis.

resorts.name: Mammoth Mountain
resorts.microclimate_note: Sits where the Sierra crest juts furthest east, catching more direct Pacific moisture than resorts to the north; its very high base (7,953ft) keeps most storms snow rather than rain even when the freezing level runs warm.

resorts.name: Palisades Tahoe
resorts.microclimate_note: Lake Tahoe's own basin effect adds a lake-enhancement layer on top of standard Sierra orographic lift, and its north-facing bowls hold powder longer than Tahoe's south-shore resorts.

resorts.name: Big Bear (Bear Mountain)
resorts.microclimate_note: The southernmost, lowest-elevation (6,750ft base) major Sierra resort — depends on colder-than-typical storm tracks reaching Southern California, making it the most rain-line-vulnerable resort in the region.

resorts.name: Northstar California
resorts.microclimate_note: Tucked on Tahoe's lee side, sheltered from the worst wind but also from some of the heaviest west-facing Sierra cement — smaller totals than Kirkwood, but better-preserved snow.

resorts.name: Kirkwood
resorts.microclimate_note: The highest and most storm-exposed of the Tahoe-area resorts, sitting in its own bowl south of the lake that consistently outperforms Tahoe's north shore for snowfall totals.

resorts.name: June Mountain
resorts.microclimate_note: Mammoth's quieter neighbor a few miles north, sharing the same high-elevation southern-Sierra exposure with far less skier traffic.

el_nino.narrative: The southern jet corridor rewards this region most consistently in El Niño years. High base elevations mean the warmer airmass still falls as snow. Taos is one of the very few major destinations where El Niño is a documented, reliable positive signal.
el_nino.caveat: A Super El Niño amplifies this signal materially — Wolf Creek and the San Juans could see exceptional seasons.

la_nina.narrative: The mirror image of the El Niño case. The southern jet corridor that fuels this region shuts off in La Niña — this is the classic 'Southwest drought' pattern, well documented across recent multi-year La Niña stretches.
la_nina.caveat: This is one of the more reliable bearish ENSO signals in North American skiing. Treat La Niña as a real headwind for the San Juans, not noise.

neutral.narrative: Without El Niño's southern jet boost, this region reverts to its normal high-variance pattern — high base elevations still help catch whatever does fall.
neutral.caveat: Track individual storm systems rather than a seasonal thesis.

resorts.name: Taos Ski Valley
resorts.microclimate_note: Sits in a gap in the Sangre de Cristo range that still catches southern-jet moisture — a unusual microclimate for northern New Mexico, and the reason it's one of the few reliable El Niño winners.

resorts.name: Wolf Creek
resorts.microclimate_note: Colorado's snowiest resort on average, sitting directly in the path of southwest-flow moisture funneling up the San Juans before any other range intercepts it — first in line for whatever the southern jet delivers.

resorts.name: Telluride
resorts.microclimate_note: A deep box-canyon setting plus a very high summit (13,150ft) gives it some of the best snow preservation in Colorado, even though the historic town itself sits comparatively low.

resorts.name: Purgatory
resorts.microclimate_note: Northern San Juans — gets a blend of southern-jet moisture and the same northern storm track that feeds Wolf Creek, without Wolf Creek's extreme single-point exposure.

resorts.name: Ski Santa Fe
resorts.microclimate_note: One of the southernmost lift-served resorts on the continent; only works at all because of its high base (10,350ft) — margin for error is thin regardless of ENSO phase.

resorts.name: Arizona Snowbowl
resorts.microclimate_note: At 35°N, one of the southernmost lift-served resorts on the continent — only works because the San Francisco Peaks punch up to 12,600ft. A marginal, high-variance climate in any ENSO phase.

el_nino.narrative: ENSO has minimal predictive power here in any phase — the correlation is statistically negligible across 50+ seasons. Don't credit or blame El Niño for however this season turns out.
el_nino.caveat: The popular narrative that El Niño reliably helps the Rockies is largely the 1982-83 halo effect. The data does not support it for Alta or the I-70 corridor.

la_nina.narrative: Same story as El Niño years: this region sits in the seam between the northern and southern storm tracks, and the ENSO correlation is negligible in either direction across 50+ seasons.
la_nina.caveat: Prior-season base snowpack and individual storm timing matter far more here than ENSO phase.

neutral.narrative: This is close to what Utah/Central Colorado looks like in every ENSO phase — the region just isn't a strong ENSO responder.
neutral.caveat: Look at the live snowpack numbers below rather than the ENSO thesis for this region.

resorts.name: Alta
resorts.microclimate_note: Little Cottonwood Canyon's uniquely funnel-shaped orientation is the textbook explanation for the Wasatch's famously light, frequent snow, with lake-effect enhancement off the Great Salt Lake layered on top.

resorts.name: Snowbird
resorts.microclimate_note: Shares Little Cottonwood Canyon with Alta and the same lake-effect mechanism, but sits slightly lower and more wind-exposed on the canyon's south side.

resorts.name: Park City
resorts.microclimate_note: Sits in a side canyon east of the main Wasatch crest, meaning it catches meaningfully less of the Cottonwood Canyons' lake-effect enhancement than Alta or Snowbird.

resorts.name: Deer Valley
resorts.microclimate_note: Adjacent to Park City with a similar exposure profile; historically built around grooming and consistency rather than the deepest powder days.

resorts.name: Breckenridge
resorts.microclimate_note: High base (9,600ft) on the Tenmile Range's east side — the leeward side of the Continental Divide for Pacific storms, so it leans more on upslope/continental systems than Colorado's wetter west-slope resorts.

resorts.name: Vail
resorts.microclimate_note: A long east-west ridge with enormous sidecountry catchment, sitting close enough to the Divide to catch decent Pacific-influenced snow before Colorado's typical continental dry-out sets in further east.

resorts.name: Steamboat
resorts.microclimate_note: The Park Range's orientation wrings moisture from Pacific storms unusually efficiently — the documented mechanism behind trademarked 'Champagne Powder,' with snow averaging roughly 6% water content versus ~15% typical elsewhere in Colorado.

resorts.name: Aspen Snowmass
resorts.microclimate_note: Central Elk Mountains with a high summit (12,510ft) but lower base; storm-track geometry here is more favorable than Crested Butte's despite similar latitude, and average snowfall (~300in) runs well above it.

resorts.name: Winter Park
resorts.microclimate_note: Sits directly on the Continental Divide via the Moffat Tunnel corridor — one of the closest resorts to Denver that still catches west-slope-style snow because the ridge itself sits on the divide.

resorts.name: Copper Mountain
resorts.microclimate_note: Adjacent to Vail Pass on the west side of the Continental Divide, with similar storm exposure to Vail/Breckenridge and a naturally divided front/back-side layout that spreads snow preservation across aspects.

resorts.name: Eldora
resorts.microclimate_note: The closest major resort to Denver, on the Front Range side of the Divide — snow totals typically lag the West Slope resorts because Front Range terrain sits in a partial rain shadow.

resorts.name: Arapahoe Basin
resorts.microclimate_note: The highest base elevation of any US lift-served resort (10,520ft) — this alone makes it one of the most temperature-buffered resorts in the country, often extending the season into June.

resorts.name: Crested Butte
resorts.microclimate_note: A continental snow climate — cold, clear, infrequent but heavy storms, and a shallower, weaker-layered snowpack than the Wasatch's more variable climate. Average annual snowfall (~208in) trails Aspen's (~300in) despite comparable elevation.

resorts.name: Solitude
resorts.microclimate_note: Sits one canyon over from Alta/Snowbird (Big Cottonwood vs. Little Cottonwood) — the same Great Salt Lake-effect mechanism applies, with a slightly less extreme funnel orientation.

resorts.name: Snowbasin
resorts.microclimate_note: The northernmost Wasatch resort in this list, catching more direct Pacific storm tracks before they reach the more sheltered central Wasatch canyons.

el_nino.narrative: The most consistently disfavored North American region in El Niño years. El Niño deflects Pacific systems south, cutting off the storm parade that defines these mountains in La Niña years.
el_nino.caveat: Grand Targhee and Big Sky show less ENSO sensitivity due to microclimatic factors. High-elevation terrain can still deliver good individual cycles.

la_nina.narrative: The Pacific Northwest and Northern Rockies are La Niña's single most reliable domestic beneficiary. The storm track locks on, and this region has produced some of its deepest seasons on record in La Niña years.
la_nina.caveat: This is one of the highest-conviction bullish ENSO signals in North American skiing. A strong La Niña can push totals well above the +15–25% base case.

neutral.narrative: Without La Niña's storm-track lock-in, the Pacific Northwest reverts to a fairly typical season — still one of the snowiest regions in North America on baseline climatology alone.
neutral.caveat: This region's normal average is high enough that 'neutral' still usually means a good season by national standards.

resorts.name: Jackson Hole
resorts.microclimate_note: The Teton Range's sheer vertical relief creates its own orographic enhancement largely independent of the broader ENSO pattern — part of why it holds up better than the regional average in unfavorable ENSO years.

resorts.name: Big Sky
resorts.microclimate_note: Montana's more continental position means lighter, drier snow than the coastal Cascades resorts, with a very high, wind-exposed summit (11,166ft).

resorts.name: Mt. Bachelor
resorts.microclimate_note: A near-perfectly conical, isolated volcano with no upwind terrain to steal moisture first — it takes the full, unfiltered brunt of any Pacific storm reaching central Oregon, for better or worse.

resorts.name: Stevens Pass
resorts.microclimate_note: Sits almost exactly on the Washington Cascades crest, making it one of the most directly storm-exposed resorts in the entire Pacific Northwest.

resorts.name: Crystal Mountain
resorts.microclimate_note: Just east of Mt. Rainier, which can shadow or enhance incoming storms depending on wind direction — a notably variable microclimate even by Cascades standards.

resorts.name: Sun Valley
resorts.microclimate_note: Idaho's more continental, drier climate than the coastal Cascades — known for consistent sunny-day powder rather than the heaviest raw totals.

resorts.name: Schweitzer
resorts.microclimate_note: Far northern Idaho panhandle, close enough to the Pacific moisture corridor to catch meaningfully more snow than Sun Valley despite being in the same state.

resorts.name: Alyeska
resorts.microclimate_note: A coastal Alaska maritime climate entirely its own — extremely heavy, wet, reliable snowfall driven by the Gulf of Alaska rather than the Pacific Northwest storm track that governs the rest of this region's ENSO signal.

resorts.name: Summit at Snoqualmie
resorts.microclimate_note: Lower elevation and closer to Seattle than Stevens Pass, making it the most rain-line-vulnerable resort in the Washington Cascades.

resorts.name: Grand Targhee
resorts.microclimate_note: Sits on the windward (west) side of the Tetons, opposite Jackson Hole — why it consistently catches more total snowfall than Jackson despite sitting right next door.

el_nino.narrative: El Niño suppresses Arctic cold intrusions, compressing both the front and back of the snow window. The 2015-16 Super El Niño drove snowfall 30–40% below average at major New England resorts.
el_nino.caveat: Negative NAO events can still produce intense Nor'easters. Book deposits, not airfare. Watch the CPC NAO index in December–January.

la_nina.narrative: La Niña doesn't suppress Arctic outbreaks the way El Niño does, so the Northeast's snow window tends to run closer to normal. It's a secondary effect, though — the NAO and AO do most of the real work in this region regardless of ENSO phase.
la_nina.caveat: Don't treat La Niña as a strong green light here — it mainly just removes El Niño's headwind rather than creating a tailwind of its own.

neutral.narrative: The Northeast is dominated by the NAO/AO regardless of ENSO phase, so a neutral ENSO year looks much like an average year here.
neutral.caveat: Watch the NAO index week to week during the season — it matters more than ENSO for this region.

negative.narrative: Negative NAO is the single best predictor of a good Northeast ski season. It favors cold-air intrusions and raises the odds of Nor'easters tracking up the coast — the storm type that makes New England's season, far more reliably than any ENSO phase.
negative.caveat: Even a negative NAO doesn't guarantee it — Nor'easter tracks are still highly storm-by-storm. But the backdrop is favorable, more so than anything ENSO tells you about this region.

neutral.narrative: Without a strong NAO signal in either direction, expect a fairly typical Northeast season. ENSO's own influence here is minor regardless of which phase it's in.
neutral.caveat: Keep watching the NAO through the season — it can swing sharply week to week even when the monthly average looks neutral.

positive.narrative: Positive NAO is the Northeast's most reliable bearish signal. It keeps the storm track and cold air locked north over Canada, producing a milder, more rain-prone pattern that compresses the season from both ends.
positive.caveat: A positive NAO doesn't rule out a single extreme storm — some of the region's biggest Nor'easters on record happened outside a clean negative-NAO winter, so don't read this as 'no snow is possible.' The correlation is also weaker in northern Maine and northern Vermont (Sugarloaf, Jay Peak), where research shows NAO's signal gets blurred by lake-effect and terrain influences that work regardless of phase — this bearish call applies most cleanly to central/southern New England (Killington, Stowe, Sugarbush, Sunday River, Cannon).

resorts.name: Killington
resorts.microclimate_note: Vermont's highest lift-served terrain and the largest snowmaking system in the East — built specifically to buffer against the region's inherent NAO-driven storm-to-storm variability.

resorts.name: Stowe
resorts.microclimate_note: Northern Vermont, closer to the Canadian border, tends to run colder than southern Vermont resorts during the same storm system.

resorts.name: Jay Peak
resorts.microclimate_note: The northernmost major Vermont resort, right on the Canadian border, catching genuine northwest-flow upslope snow that resorts further south miss — one of the snowiest resorts in the East on average.

resorts.name: Cannon Mountain
resorts.microclimate_note: An exposed, high-elevation White Mountains site with less snowmaking reliance historically than most Northeast resorts — more weather-dependent than the regional norm.

resorts.name: Sugarbush
resorts.microclimate_note: Central Vermont, a similar exposure profile to Stowe and Killington, historically less snowmaking-dependent thanks to favorable natural terrain.

resorts.name: Sunday River
resorts.microclimate_note: Maine's eight interconnected peaks spread storm exposure across a wide east-west footprint, buffering against any single storm's track missing part of the resort.

resorts.name: Sugarloaf
resorts.microclimate_note: Maine's highest lift-served peak, exposed enough for above-treeline skiing — the most alpine, wind-affected terrain profile in the Northeast.

resorts.name: Okemo
resorts.microclimate_note: Southern Vermont — historically the most snowmaking-dependent of the state's major resorts given its lower elevation and more southerly exposure.

resorts.name: Mount Snow
resorts.microclimate_note: The southernmost major Vermont resort — the most exposed of the state's resorts to the region's rain-line risk in marginal storms.

resorts.name: Mount Sunapee
resorts.microclimate_note: South-central New Hampshire, lower elevation — generally the most temperature-marginal resort among this NH cluster.

resorts.name: Attitash
resorts.microclimate_note: White Mountains, moderate elevation, sitting in a valley that can trap cold air during Arctic outbreaks.

resorts.name: Wildcat
resorts.microclimate_note: Sits directly across the valley from Mt. Washington — one of the most wind-exposed, coldest resorts in the East, benefiting from proximity to the most extreme weather station in the region.

resorts.name: Hunter Mountain
resorts.microclimate_note: Catskills, New York — the southernmost, lowest-elevation major resort in this list, and correspondingly the most snowmaking-dependent.

resorts.name: Stratton
resorts.microclimate_note: Southern Vermont, a similar exposure profile to Okemo and Mount Snow — lower elevation makes it more rain-line-sensitive than northern Vermont resorts.

resorts.name: Loon Mountain
resorts.microclimate_note: White Mountains, New Hampshire — moderate elevation with heavy snowmaking investment to smooth out natural variability.

resorts.name: Snowshoe
resorts.microclimate_note: The southernmost resort in this region by a wide margin — its unusually high base for the Appalachians (3,370ft) is the only reason it functions as a ski area at all.

resorts.name: Tremblant
resorts.microclimate_note: Quebec's Laurentians sit further from the immediate Atlantic coastal storm track than New England, catching more Great Lakes and continental Arctic influence instead — a distinct microclimate from the rest of this NAO-driven region, generally colder and more temperature-consistent.

el_nino.narrative: La Niña's top beneficiary becomes El Niño's clearest loser in North America. BC interior is almost entirely Pacific storm-track dependent, and El Niño cuts that track off.
el_nino.caveat: A Super El Niño amplifies this signal materially. If the tail scenario confirms, avoid non-refundable BC interior bookings.

la_nina.narrative: BC interior — Revelstoke, Big White — is La Niña's top North American beneficiary, almost entirely because of how directly it sits in the enhanced Pacific storm track. Coastal Whistler benefits too, though slightly less dramatically thanks to its own orographic lift baseline.
la_nina.caveat: This is a high-conviction bullish signal — among the strongest ENSO-ski correlations anywhere in North America.

neutral.narrative: Without La Niña's storm-track lock-in, expect something closer to this region's long-run average — still generally snowy given the baseline climatology.
neutral.caveat: Local orographic effects (coastal vs. interior) matter more than ENSO in a neutral year.

resorts.name: Whistler Blackcomb
resorts.microclimate_note: A coastal maritime climate with huge vertical (5,000+ft) spanning multiple microclimates in a single mountain, from rainforest base to alpine bowl — a famously wide temperature and precipitation range.

resorts.name: Revelstoke
resorts.microclimate_note: Deep interior BC with some of the highest average snowfall totals in North America, driven by moist Pacific flow funneled through the Columbia Mountains with no coastal range to intercept it first.

resorts.name: Banff / Lake Louise
resorts.microclimate_note: East of the Continental Divide in the true Canadian Rockies — drier and colder than the BC interior resorts, a different, more continental climate than Revelstoke or Whistler despite the shared region label.

resorts.name: Big White
resorts.microclimate_note: High base elevation for BC-interior standards, known for exceptionally light snow and thick rime 'snow ghost' formations built up by persistent cloud inversions.

resorts.name: Sun Peaks
resorts.microclimate_note: Rain-shadowed by the Coast and Columbia Mountains, giving it a notably drier, sunnier climate than Whistler or Revelstoke despite similar latitude.

resorts.name: Kicking Horse
resorts.microclimate_note: Continental-Divide-adjacent in the Purcell Mountains, with very high vertical and alpine bowls that hold snow exceptionally well once it falls.

resorts.name: Fernie
resorts.microclimate_note: Southeastern BC, sitting in its own snow-catching bowl (locally 'the Fernie Alps') known for localized storm enhancement distinct from the broader regional pattern.

resorts.name: Panorama
resorts.microclimate_note: Purcell Mountains, further from the primary Pacific storm track than Revelstoke or Whistler — a drier interior climate known for excellent grooming reliability.

resorts.name: SilverStar
resorts.microclimate_note: Sits on a rain-shadow ridge above Vernon — famous for extremely light, dry snow despite its BC-interior geography.

resorts.name: RED Mountain
resorts.microclimate_note: Southern BC near the US border, in the same general moisture corridor as Schweitzer and Whitefish across the border — deep, consistent interior snowfall.

resorts.name: Cypress
resorts.microclimate_note: The most coastal, lowest-elevation, most maritime of the BC resorts here — closest in character to Whistler's base but smaller and more rain-line-vulnerable given its 2,600ft base.

el_nino.narrative: Historical data shows little consistent ENSO-snowfall correlation in the Alps — the NAO is the dominant driver. El Niño's main risk is indirect: warmer background conditions raising the rain-snow line at lower resorts. Above 2,500m the signal is negligible.
el_nino.caveat: Book high. A Sudden Stratospheric Warming event mid-winter can override El Niño for 4–6 weeks — SSW probability rises with low Arctic sea ice extent.

la_nina.narrative: ENSO's influence on European winters is faint in either phase — the NAO and polar vortex configuration matter far more. La Niña winters show a marginal lean toward a more meridional (blocky) jet pattern, which can help or hurt the Alps depending on where the blocking sets up.
la_nina.caveat: Book high regardless of ENSO phase — elevation is the dominant variable here, not the Pacific.

neutral.narrative: The Alps are an NAO-driven region in every ENSO phase, so a neutral year looks much like any other year here.
neutral.caveat: Watch the NAO/polar vortex state through the season — it's the signal that matters for the Alps.

negative.narrative: Negative NAO weakens the usual west-to-east Atlantic storm track and lets cold air push further south into central Europe — the pattern most associated with good, reliable Alpine snow, including at lower and southern-facing resorts.
negative.caveat: Negative NAO winters are also more prone to blocking-driven dry spells between cold outbreaks — snow tends to arrive in bursts rather than a steady parade of storms. Still worth booking high as insurance.

neutral.narrative: Without a strong NAO signal, the Alps default to elevation-dependent noise — no consistent tilt toward more or less snow. ENSO's own influence here is negligible in any phase.
neutral.caveat: Book high regardless — elevation is the dominant variable when the NAO isn't giving a clear signal.

positive.narrative: Positive NAO drives a strong, mild westerly flow across northern Europe. For the Alps that typically means a higher freezing level and reduced snow reliability at lower resorts — the riskier pattern for anything below roughly 2,000m.
positive.caveat: Above 2,500m the signal is much weaker — glacier and high-altitude terrain (Zermatt's upper lifts, Val d'Isère's glacier) hold up fine even in a positive-NAO winter.

resorts.name: Zermatt
resorts.microclimate_note: Extremely high, glaciated terrain (base 5,310ft, summit 12,740ft at Matterhorn Glacier Paradise) makes it one of the least NAO-sensitive resorts in the Alps at altitude — skiable year-round on the glacier regardless of the winter's overall pattern.

resorts.name: Val d'Isère
resorts.microclimate_note: Part of the Espace Killy with Tignes, high-altitude (6,070ft base) with a north-facing orientation that holds snow well; historically runs its own local pass rather than joining Epic or Ikon.

resorts.name: St. Anton
resorts.microclimate_note: The Arlberg region catches an outsized share of Atlantic moisture crossing directly into western Austria before it's wrung out further east — one of the snowiest low-to-mid elevation zones in the Alps.

resorts.name: Chamonix
resorts.microclimate_note: Sits directly beneath Mont Blanc's massive relief, creating intense localized orographic lift — famous for advanced/off-piste terrain rather than groomed-piste snow reliability.

resorts.name: Verbier
resorts.microclimate_note: Part of the large interconnected 4 Vallées system, with highly varied aspect and elevation across its four valleys that buffers against any single slope's bad exposure in a given storm.

resorts.name: Les Trois Vallées (Courchevel / Méribel / Val Thorens)
resorts.microclimate_note: The world's largest lift-connected ski area; Val Thorens alone sits above 3,200m, giving the system's upper reaches strong snow reliability even when Courchevel's lower village-level slopes run marginal.

resorts.name: Kitzbühel
resorts.microclimate_note: Relatively low elevation for the Alps (2,500ft base) and known for snowmaking dependence on the lower Hahnenkamm slopes — one of the more temperature-vulnerable major Austrian resorts.

resorts.name: St. Moritz
resorts.microclimate_note: High-altitude Engadin valley in eastern Switzerland — drier and sunnier than the western Alps due to its more continental position, reliably cold but historically lighter on total snowfall than Zermatt or Verbier.

resorts.name: Sölden
resorts.microclimate_note: A glacier resort (Rettenbach/Tiefenbach) with reliable autumn and high-elevation snow independent of the main winter pattern, extending its effective season well beyond the NAO-driven core months.

resorts.name: Saalbach
resorts.microclimate_note: Salzburg region, moderate elevation, heavily snowmaking-supported, sitting in a similar moisture path to Kitzbühel.

resorts.name: Zell am See-Kaprun
resorts.microclimate_note: Combines a lower valley resort with the high-altitude Kitzsteinhorn glacier (9,928ft) — the glacier portion is largely NAO-independent, similar to Sölden's setup.

resorts.name: Mayrhofen
resorts.microclimate_note: Zillertal valley, Tyrol — moderate elevation with a high-altitude glacier extension nearby (Hintertux) providing a similar buffer to Zell am See's setup.

resorts.name: Andermatt
resorts.microclimate_note: Central Swiss Alps, historically one of the snowiest towns in Switzerland due to its position where several Alpine passes converge and funnel moisture.

resorts.name: Ischgl
resorts.microclimate_note: Paznaun valley, a high base for Austria (4,610ft) with strong snow reliability and famously extensive snowmaking as backup.

resorts.name: Grandvalira
resorts.microclimate_note: Andorra's Pyrenees location is a different mountain range from the Alps — more Atlantic/Mediterranean-influenced, generally less snow-reliable than the high Alps, but the largest ski area in the Pyrenees.

resorts.name: Cortina d'Ampezzo
resorts.microclimate_note: The Dolomites' more continental-Mediterranean position makes them drier and notably sunnier than the western Alps (sun roughly 8 days out of 10) — reliable high-altitude accumulation but historically thinner cover at lower village elevations, offset by heavy snowmaking.

resorts.name: Madonna di Campiglio
resorts.microclimate_note: Western Dolomites, sharing Cortina's continental-Mediterranean character but in a slightly more sheltered, lower-profile setting.

el_nino.narrative: Japan defies the North American intuition. Niseko showed above-average snowfall in 7 of 12 El Niño cycles since 1954. Japan's powder is driven by Siberian cold air crossing the Sea of Japan — a mechanism only weakly coupled to ENSO. Hakuba is the notable exception: below average in ~83% of El Niño years.
el_nino.caveat: For Japan-focused skiers: Niseko holds up historically. Hakuba is a meaningful risk in this ENSO regime.

la_nina.narrative: La Niña strengthens the Siberian High and the East Asian winter monsoon, generally increasing cold-air outbreaks across the Sea of Japan — the exact mechanism behind Japan's famous powder. This is historically the more reliable phase for Japan overall, including at Hakuba.
la_nina.caveat: Still a continental cold-air mechanism, not a Pacific one — expect a good baseline rather than a dramatic swing.

neutral.narrative: Japan's snow machine runs mostly on the East Asian winter monsoon rather than ENSO, so a neutral year tracks close to the long-run baseline — which is already very good by global standards.
neutral.caveat: Local sea-surface temperature in the Sea of Japan matters more than ENSO phase for a given week's dump.

resorts.name: Niseko United
resorts.microclimate_note: Directly downwind of the Sea of Japan with no upwind terrain to intercept Siberian moisture first — about as ENSO-independent a snow machine as exists anywhere, driven almost entirely by the Siberian High and East Asian winter monsoon.

resorts.name: Furano
resorts.microclimate_note: Interior Hokkaido, slightly more continental and sheltered than coastal Niseko, producing a drier, lighter snow than its more famous neighbor.

resorts.name: Myoko
resorts.microclimate_note: Niigata Prefecture — one of the snowiest inhabited regions on Earth by raw totals, sitting directly in the path of Sea-of-Japan moisture hitting the first major mountains it encounters.

resorts.name: Nozawa Onsen
resorts.microclimate_note: Nagano, slightly further inland than the Niigata resorts — historically reliable but with somewhat lower totals than Myoko.

resorts.name: Hakuba Valley (Happo-One)
resorts.microclimate_note: Nagano's Northern Alps, where high relief creates strong orographic enhancement — though its position further from the coast than the Niigata resorts is part of why it's the documented exception to Japan's usual El Niño resilience.

resorts.name: Rusutsu
resorts.microclimate_note: Near Niseko on Hokkaido, with similar Sea-of-Japan exposure but more sheltered, tree-lined terrain.

resorts.name: Appi Kogen
resorts.microclimate_note: Northern Honshu (Iwate), further from the Sea of Japan coast than the Niigata/Hokkaido resorts — a somewhat drier, more continental snow character as a result.

resorts.name: Shiga Kogen
resorts.microclimate_note: Nagano — one of Japan's largest ski areas by skiable terrain, with a high base elevation for Honshu standards that helps snow reliability.

el_nino.narrative: The clearest El Niño beneficiary globally. The high central Andes respond to El Niño more directly than almost any other ski region on earth. Portillo is the highest-conviction destination in a strong El Niño cycle. Season: June–September; peak window July–mid-August.
el_nino.caveat: A Super El Niño is a structural long for Portillo. Book early — El Niño years generate unusual Northern Hemisphere interest in Andean destinations.

la_nina.narrative: The mirror image of the El Niño case. La Niña years bring below-average precipitation to the central Andes, sometimes severely so — central Chile's ongoing multi-year drought has coincided with a persistent La Niña-leaning Pacific.
la_nina.caveat: Highest-conviction avoid in the Southern Hemisphere during a La Niña cycle. If you're set on the Andes this phase, look at whichever resort has the highest base elevation and the healthiest snowmaking.

neutral.narrative: Without El Niño's boost or La Niña's drought pattern, the central Andes track closer to their long-run average — still a high-elevation desert climate that depends on individual frontal systems.
neutral.caveat: Check current-season snowpack directly rather than leaning on ENSO in a neutral year.

resorts.name: Portillo
resorts.microclimate_note: Sits at a natural high-Andes pass near the Argentina border, directly in the path of the frontal systems that define El Niño's Southern Hemisphere signal — the highest-conviction ENSO-responsive resort on this entire site.

resorts.name: Valle Nevado
resorts.microclimate_note: Slightly lower and closer to Santiago than Portillo, with similar frontal-system exposure but somewhat more affected by the urban/coastal transition zone.

resorts.name: Bariloche (Cerro Catedral)
resorts.microclimate_note: Northern Argentine Patagonia — a different climate regime from the desert-adjacent central Andes, more consistently humid and less dependent on any single frontal system.

resorts.name: Las Leñas
resorts.microclimate_note: Mendoza province, extremely high and exposed — known for high-wind days that can close lifts even when snow conditions themselves are excellent.

resorts.name: Nevados de Chillán
resorts.microclimate_note: Southern-central Chile, volcanic terrain, generally sitting in a wetter baseline climate than the more desert-adjacent resorts further north.

resorts.name: Cerro Castor
resorts.microclimate_note: The world's southernmost ski resort, near Ushuaia at 54.6°S — a sub-Antarctic maritime climate with a very different mechanism (Southern Ocean storm tracks) than the desert-adjacent central Andes resorts further north.

el_nino.narrative: El Niño's clearest victim globally. Warmer temperatures, reduced precipitation, early closures, and compressed seasons characterize strong El Niño winters in Australia. Marginal base elevations offer no buffer against warm-air intrusions.
el_nino.caveat: Highest-conviction avoid of any strong El Niño cycle. Season runs June–September — full overlap with the strongest Southern Hemisphere El Niño signal.

la_nina.narrative: The mirror image of the El Niño case. La Niña's wetter, cooler pattern over southeastern Australia is the best-case scenario for the Australian Alps — more consistent snowfall and later closures than an average season.
la_nina.caveat: Even a favorable La Niña doesn't fully offset Australia's low, marginal base elevations — book flexible dates rather than assuming a guaranteed deep season.

neutral.narrative: Without El Niño's warm-and-dry push or La Niña's wet-and-cool boost, Australia tracks closer to its (already marginal) long-run average.
neutral.caveat: Given how thin the margin for error already is at these elevations, check snow depth reports directly during the season.

resorts.name: Perisher
resorts.microclimate_note: New South Wales' largest ski area by terrain, but still constrained by Australia's overall marginal base elevations for snow reliability.

resorts.name: Falls Creek
resorts.microclimate_note: Victoria — known for reliable grooming and one of the more consistent snow records among the Victorian resorts.

resorts.name: Thredbo
resorts.microclimate_note: NSW's highest vertical drop gives it slightly better snow retention than the lower Victorian resorts in a marginal season.

resorts.name: Mt. Buller
resorts.microclimate_note: Victoria's resort closest to Melbourne, and historically more exposed to warm intrusions given its lower average elevation.

resorts.name: Mt. Hotham
resorts.microclimate_note: Victoria's highest resort village, generally the most snow-reliable of the Victorian options in a typical season.

negative.narrative: Negative SAM drags the Southern Ocean westerly storm belt north onto the Australian Alps — per Australia's Bureau of Meteorology this is the single strongest snowfall driver the country has, outweighing ENSO. It means more frequent cold fronts reaching the ski fields instead of passing south of them.
negative.caveat: SAM is a fast-moving pattern with only 1–3 weeks of real predictive skill, so a negative reading is a great sign for the next few weeks, not a season-long guarantee. Australia's marginal base elevations still cap the upside.

neutral.narrative: With SAM near neutral, the storm belt sits in roughly its average position and Australia's season tracks its (already marginal) long-run baseline. ENSO and IOD become the tiebreakers.
neutral.caveat: Australia has the highest year-to-year snowfall variability of any region on this site — historically a coefficient of variation around 0.50–0.56, versus roughly 0.17–0.21 in Japan. Neutral means unpredictable here, not 'safe'.

positive.narrative: Positive SAM pulls the westerly storm belt south toward Antarctica, so the cold fronts that make Australia's season track past the continent instead of over it. This is the classic setup for a thin, late-starting, early-finishing Australian winter.
positive.caveat: A positive SAM can still be punctuated by individual strong fronts — Australia's season is made of a handful of big events, so one good week can rescue a bad month. But the odds are against you.

el_nino.narrative: ENSO has little direct reach into Scandinavia. The NAO is what matters here, and it is tracked separately below.
el_nino.caveat: Ignore the ENSO number for this region and watch the NAO instead.

la_nina.narrative: As with El Niño, ENSO's influence this far north in the Atlantic sector is faint and inconsistent.
la_nina.caveat: The NAO reading is the one to act on.

neutral.narrative: A neutral Pacific says almost nothing about a Scandinavian winter.
neutral.caveat: Watch the NAO.

positive.narrative: This is the inverse of the Alps. A positive NAO drives a strong Atlantic jet that pushes the storm track north into Scandinavia, raising winter precipitation across Norway and Sweden. Scandinavian glacier mass-balance records show above-normal accumulation in positive-NAO winters.
positive.caveat: Positive NAO also brings milder air. At these latitudes it usually still falls as snow, but the low-elevation southern resorts (Trysil, parts of Åre) carry more rain risk than the far north.

neutral.narrative: Without a clear NAO signal the Atlantic storm track sits in roughly its average position and the season tracks the long-run baseline.
neutral.caveat: Elevation and latitude matter more than the seasonal signal in a neutral year.

negative.narrative: A negative NAO buckles the jet and sends Atlantic moisture south toward central and southern Europe instead. Scandinavia turns colder but noticeably drier, so cover builds slowly even though it preserves well once down.
negative.caveat: Cold is rarely Scandinavia's problem; moisture is. A negative NAO is the pattern that leaves thin cover into January.

resorts.name: Åre
resorts.microclimate_note: Scandinavia's largest ski area, on a lake-adjacent massif that catches Atlantic moisture crossing Norway. Low base elevation for its snowfall, so it depends on latitude rather than altitude for cold.

resorts.name: Hemsedal
resorts.microclimate_note: Inland southern Norway, high enough to hold cold better than the coastal resorts while still catching Atlantic systems that clear the coastal range.

resorts.name: Trysil
resorts.microclimate_note: Norway's biggest resort by terrain, well inland and in a partial rain shadow — reliably cold, but drier than the western Norwegian mountains and heavily snowmaking-supported early.

resorts.name: Riksgränsen
resorts.microclimate_note: Inside the Arctic Circle on the Norwegian border, catching maritime moisture off the Norwegian Sea. Cold is never the constraint; daylight is, which is why the season runs late and includes midnight skiing in May.

resorts.name: Levi
resorts.microclimate_note: Finnish Lapland: very low elevation but very high latitude, so the snow is dry and the season is long. Vertical is minimal — this is a cold-reliability destination, not a big-mountain one.

resorts.name: Ruka
resorts.microclimate_note: Northeastern Finland, close enough to the White Sea to pick up extra moisture. One of the longest seasons in Europe, typically October to May.

el_nino.narrative: ENSO's signal over southeastern Europe is weak and inconsistent. Mediterranean cyclone frequency, driven largely by the NAO, is the thing to watch.
el_nino.caveat: Use the NAO reading below rather than the ENSO one.

la_nina.narrative: Same as the El Niño case: little reliable ENSO influence this far east in Europe.
la_nina.caveat: The NAO reading is the useful one.

neutral.narrative: No meaningful ENSO steer for the Balkans.
neutral.caveat: Watch the NAO and the position of the Siberian high.

negative.narrative: A negative NAO pushes the Atlantic storm track south, feeding Mediterranean cyclogenesis. Those cyclones are what deliver moisture to Bulgaria, Serbia and Romania, and when that moisture meets cold air spilling off the Siberian high it falls as heavy mountain snow.
negative.caveat: The two ingredients have to arrive together. A Mediterranean cyclone without the cold air produces rain to the top of many Balkan resorts, which is the region's characteristic failure mode.

neutral.narrative: An average number of Mediterranean systems, and an average season. The Balkans lean heavily on snowmaking to bridge the gaps regardless.
neutral.caveat: Base elevation is the differentiator here — Borovets and Pamporovo start high, Bansko's village does not.

positive.narrative: A positive NAO drags the storm track north over Scandinavia and leaves southeastern Europe dry. This is the pattern that produces thin, snowmaking-dependent Balkan winters.
positive.caveat: Cold outbreaks from the east can still arrive independently, but without Mediterranean moisture there is little for them to work with.

resorts.name: Bansko
resorts.microclimate_note: The Pirin massif gives Bansko the biggest vertical in Bulgaria, but the town sits at only 990m — the gondola does the work, and the lower runs are the first to go in a mild spell.

resorts.name: Borovets
resorts.microclimate_note: Rila mountains, with a much higher base than Bansko (1,300m) and a correspondingly better cold margin. Tree-lined and sheltered, so it holds snow through wind events.

resorts.name: Pamporovo
resorts.microclimate_note: The Rhodopes, further south and closer to the Aegean, so it sees more Mediterranean moisture but also warmer airmasses. High base for the region, modest vertical.

resorts.name: Kopaonik
resorts.microclimate_note: Serbia's main resort, sitting on an exposed plateau that gets sun and wind in equal measure. Extensive snowmaking compensates for an inconsistent natural supply.

resorts.name: Poiana Brașov
resorts.microclimate_note: Southern Carpathians. More continental than the Bulgarian resorts, so colder on average but reliant on fewer, larger snowfall events.

resorts.name: Jahorina
resorts.microclimate_note: Close enough to the Adriatic to catch Mediterranean systems head-on, which makes it one of the snowier Balkan options when the southern track is active.

el_nino.narrative: No reliable ENSO signal here. These ranges run on Black Sea and Mediterranean moisture meeting continental cold, and their defence is raw altitude — most of the region's resorts start above 2,000m.
el_nino.caveat: Very high base elevations mean cold is rarely the binding constraint. Moisture delivery is.

la_nina.narrative: As with El Niño, ENSO offers little steer for the Caucasus or Anatolia.
la_nina.caveat: Judge these on altitude and on how active the Black Sea and Mediterranean storm tracks are.

neutral.narrative: A typical season, governed by local storm frequency rather than any hemispheric signal.
neutral.caveat: The high base elevations make this region less temperature-fragile than the Alps or the Balkans.

resorts.name: Gudauri
resorts.microclimate_note: On the Georgian Military Highway in the Greater Caucasus, base near 2,000m. Catches moisture pushed up from the Black Sea and holds it — one of the better snow records in the wider region.

resorts.name: Rosa Khutor
resorts.microclimate_note: Western Caucasus, only 40km from the Black Sea, which makes it unusually maritime for the region: heavy snowfall up high, but a low base at 940m that sees rain in mild spells.

resorts.name: Palandöken
resorts.microclimate_note: Eastern Anatolia at 2,200m base, high and continental. Very cold and dry — light snow, reliable cover, and long fall-line pistes straight above Erzurum.

resorts.name: Erciyes
resorts.microclimate_note: An isolated volcano rising off the central Anatolian plateau, so it takes storms unfiltered from any direction, but sits in a dry continental climate that limits total accumulation.

el_nino.narrative: The Tien Shan sits deep inside the Eurasian landmass with no reliable ENSO teleconnection. It is reliably cold and reliably high; what varies is how much moisture reaches it from the west.
el_nino.caveat: Snow quality here is excellent and snow quantity is modest. This is a continental snowpack in the fullest sense.

la_nina.narrative: No usable ENSO steer. Westerly disturbances crossing the Caspian are the moisture source, and their frequency is not well predicted by the Pacific.
la_nina.caveat: Judge on elevation and on recent storm activity rather than on any seasonal index.

neutral.narrative: A typical Tien Shan season: cold throughout, light dry snow, and totals well below any maritime range.
neutral.caveat: Access and avalanche conditions are usually the limiting factors here rather than snow cover.

resorts.name: Shymbulak
resorts.microclimate_note: In the Zailiysky Alatau directly above Almaty, base at 2,260m. Deep continental cold with a dry, light snowpack, and a season that runs long because nothing melts.

resorts.name: Karakol
resorts.microclimate_note: Above Lake Issyk-Kul in the Tien Shan. The lake adds a modest moisture source that the rest of Central Asia lacks, giving Karakol a better snow record than its longitude suggests.

el_nino.narrative: New Zealand runs opposite to Australia under El Niño. Higher pressure over Australia drives a persistent southwesterly airstream onto the South Island, and that flow is what loads the western and southern Southern Alps. The Queenstown and Wanaka fields sit directly in it.
el_nino.caveat: The same pattern leaves the north and east of the country wanting, so Mt Hutt in Canterbury benefits far less than the Queenstown fields. ENSO also explains under a quarter of New Zealand's seasonal variance, so this is a lean, not a lock.

la_nina.narrative: La Niña tends toward more northeasterly flow, which is warmer and aimed at the wrong side of the island for the main ski fields. The southwest loses its reliable feed.
la_nina.caveat: Not a washout — northeast flow can still deliver to Canterbury fields like Mt Hutt, roughly inverting the El Niño pattern.

neutral.narrative: Without an ENSO steer, New Zealand's season comes down to how often southwest fronts arrive, which is largely a SAM question week to week.
neutral.caveat: Watch SAM. It moves fast enough to make or break a fortnight regardless of the seasonal background.

resorts.name: Coronet Peak
resorts.microclimate_note: Closest field to Queenstown and the most exposed to southwest fronts, but also the lowest of the Queenstown group — the first to suffer when the freezing level lifts.

resorts.name: The Remarkables
resorts.microclimate_note: A high basin above Queenstown with a 1,586m base, the best cold margin of the Queenstown fields and a natural bowl that holds wind-blown snow.

resorts.name: Cardrona
resorts.microclimate_note: On a sunny, sheltered basin between Wanaka and Queenstown. Drier and less storm-battered than Treble Cone, with snowmaking across the main trails.

resorts.name: Treble Cone
resorts.microclimate_note: The most westerly major field, facing the Southern Alps divide, so it takes southwest storms first and hardest. Steepest terrain in the country and the biggest single vertical.

resorts.name: Mt Hutt
resorts.microclimate_note: Canterbury, on the eastern side of the divide, so it works on a different flow to the Queenstown fields — better in northeasterly patterns, weaker in the southwesterlies El Niño favours.

el_nino.narrative: These resorts run on the East Asian winter monsoon, the same cold-air engine that feeds Japan. El Niño tends to weaken the Siberian High and the monsoon flow, which means fewer and milder cold surges.
el_nino.caveat: Unlike Japan, Korea and northern China sit on the dry side of the Sea of Japan and get little lake-effect equivalent, so a weaker monsoon hits them harder. Snowmaking carries most resorts here regardless.

la_nina.narrative: La Niña strengthens the Siberian High and the East Asian winter monsoon, delivering more frequent and colder outbreaks across the Korean peninsula and northern China.
la_nina.caveat: More cold does not automatically mean more snow here — it mostly means snowmaking works better and for longer.

neutral.narrative: A typical monsoon season. Cold is generally dependable; natural snowfall is modest and heavily supplemented.
neutral.caveat: Treat published snowfall figures cautiously — most terrain here is machine-made.

resorts.name: Yongpyong
resorts.microclimate_note: Korea's largest resort, in the Taebaek range where cold monsoon air crossing the Yellow Sea picks up just enough moisture to produce genuine natural snowfall — more than the rest of the peninsula.

resorts.name: Yabuli
resorts.microclimate_note: Heilongjiang, deep in northeastern China. Bitterly cold and very dry, with the longest vertical in the country but modest natural accumulation.

resorts.name: Chongli (Genting)
resorts.microclimate_note: The 2022 Olympic freestyle venue northwest of Beijing, on the edge of the Mongolian plateau. Reliably cold and almost entirely machine-made — natural snowfall here is minimal.
